chapters.title: Chapter 6: Cash Flow Management in Practice

lessons.title: Case Study: Diagnosing and Fixing a Cash Crisis in an Indian Business

children.text: This final lesson puts everything together on one company. Vidarbha Engineering, the fictional Nagpur component maker from Lesson 6.2, has reached the point where the numbers stopped being a warning and became a problem. Nothing in the fix requires new theory. Every tool used here has appeared somewhere in the last seventeen lessons, which is rather the point: a cash crisis is almost never solved by a clever instrument, it is solved by doing ordinary things in the right order, fast.

body.text: In a cash crisis, sequence matters more than brilliance. Stabilise first, diagnose properly, fix the structure, then change the system that allowed it. Companies that reverse those steps run out of time.

children.text: Vidarbha Engineering supplies machined components to two large automotive customers and a handful of smaller buyers. Annual turnover is ₹80 crore, cost of goods sold ₹56 crore, and the company earned ₹5.2 crore of profit after tax last year. It is profitable, it has grown every year, and it cannot pay its bills.

cells: Up from 83 days six quarters ago
96 days of sales, of which ₹6 crore is overdue
98 days, including ₹1.2 crore not moved in a year
92 days, including ₹2.4 crore owed to micro and small suppliers beyond the statutory limit
At the ceiling for four months, renewal due in 60 days
GST paid nine days late last month
The first slip in the company's history
Salaries went out three days late

stats.label: Cash absorbed by the cycle
stats.context: Working capital rose from ₹16.55 to ₹21.96 crore

stats.label: Borrowing headroom
stats.context: Limit fully drawn, drawing power falling as receivables age

body.text: Read those three numbers together and the diagnosis writes itself. Six quarters of profit went into receivables and inventory instead of the bank, roughly a year of earnings, and the funding for it came from a facility that is now exhausted and from suppliers who have stopped agreeing. This is not a profitability problem and no amount of extra sales will fix it.

children.text: The first phase has one objective, which is to stop the business failing while the real fix is built. Nothing structural gets solved in ninety days.

events.title: See the position
events.description: Build the 13-week forecast from Lesson 4.2, from the actual bank statement. Freeze all discretionary spending and capex. Establish one rule: statutory dues are funded first, always, starting this month.

events.title: Collections war room
events.description: Every account beyond 60 days gets an owner, a date and a daily call-over. The promoter personally calls the two largest overdue accounts. Supply stops to anyone two invoices behind.

events.title: Protect the supply chain
events.description: Micro and small suppliers are paid first, because delaying them carries MSMED interest, disallowance and a public filing. Large suppliers get a written, dated schedule rather than silence.

events.title: Convert what is already there
events.description: Discount accepted invoices from the two large automotive customers, or route them through TReDS. Clear dead stock at whatever it fetches.

events.title: Talk to the bank early
events.description: Go in before the renewal with the forecast, the working capital plan and the collections data. A bank told in advance behaves very differently from a bank that discovers it.

events.title: Hold the discipline
events.description: Weekly cash meeting, forecast against actual every week, and no return to old payment habits as soon as the balance improves.

body.title: Cash raised or preserved in ninety days (₹ crore)

children.text: That is ₹6.9 crore of room created in a quarter, and not one rupee of it came from a new lender. Three of the four actions simply converted assets the company already owned into cash, and the fourth stopped money leaving.

body.text: Notice what is absent from the ninety-day plan. No delay of statutory dues, and no stretching of micro and small suppliers. Both would have released cash quickly and both were refused, because each carries interest that cannot be deducted, a disallowed expense, a public filing, and a supply chain that stops working exactly when the company needs it most.

body.title: Day one
body.question: You are brought in on day one. Which of these do you do first?
options: Approach three NBFCs for an emergency unsecured facility
Build a 13-week cash forecast from the bank statement and freeze discretionary spending
Call a management meeting to discuss cost reduction targets for the year
Instruct accounts to delay all supplier payments by 30 days while the position is assessed
body.explanation: You cannot manage what you cannot see, and every other decision depends on knowing the trough and its date. Emergency borrowing before the diagnosis funds the symptom at the worst available price. Annual cost targets are a twelve-month conversation, not a ninety-day one. A blanket payment delay is precisely the move that triggers MSMED consequences and supply stoppages.

children.text: Stabilisation buys time. The structural work is the same three levers from Chapter 3, with targets that are demanding but ordinary for this industry.

cells: Credit limits enforced, supply stopped for defaulters, commission linked to collection
Dead stock cleared, slow items delisted, buffers set by item rather than a blanket policy
Paying properly again, within statutory limits, with terms negotiated openly
Working capital falls from ₹21.96 crore to about ₹16.56 crore

body.text: The payables line is the one most plans leave out, and it is the reason many turnarounds relapse. Normalising supplier payment consumes ₹4.91 crore of the cash the other two levers release. A plan that quietly keeps suppliers stretched looks better on paper and simply defers the reckoning, usually to the moment a key supplier decides it has had enough.

stats.label: Cycle
stats.context: Still above the 83 days of two years ago

body.title: Size one lever
body.prompt: Vidarbha Engineering has annual sales of ₹80 crore. If debtor days fall from 96 to 65, how much cash does that release, in ₹ crore? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: One day of sales is ₹80 crore divided by 365, about ₹21.92 lakh. Thirty-one days released is about ₹6.80 crore. That single lever is larger than the entire ninety-day stabilisation plan, which is why collections discipline is the first structural priority in almost every Indian turnaround.

children.text: Working capital improvements decay. Within eighteen months, most companies that fix a cycle without fixing the system are back where they started, because nothing changed about how decisions get made.

columns.label: Before
points: Credit terms agreed by whoever closed the deal
Cash discussed monthly, after the fact
Procurement measured on unit price alone
Warning metrics reviewed once a year, at audit
Statutory payments funded from whatever was left

columns.label: After
points: Credit limits approved outside the sales line
Thirty-minute cash meeting every Monday on a rolling 13-week forecast
Procurement measured on total cost including carrying cost
Cycle, ageing and cash conversion reviewed monthly by the board
Statutory dues swept aside on the 1st, before anything else

body.title: What if the ninety days are not enough?

children.text: Sometimes the gap is too large to close operationally, and it is worth knowing what the landscape looks like before it is reached rather than during.
Banks have far more options before an account is classified than after, which is why the Lesson 6.2 timeline matters so much. Go early, with data.
Promoter infusion, a strategic investor, or the sale of a non-core asset such as surplus land or an idle machine. Slow, but it fixes the balance sheet rather than the symptom.

Under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, the minimum default for initiating a corporate insolvency resolution process was raised to ₹1 crore by a notification dated 24 March 2020, and applications can be brought by financial creditors under Section 7 or operational creditors under Section 9. A separate pre-packaged process exists for corporate MSMEs.

The practical point for a manager is simple: an unpaid operational creditor can act, and the threshold is a business-sized number rather than a symbolic one. That is one more reason a written, dated payment schedule with a large supplier is worth far more than silence and hope. Any actual insolvency question needs qualified legal advice, not a course.

body.title: The order of work
body.textWithBlank: In a cash crisis the correct sequence is: stabilise, diagnose, fix the structure, then change the ___ that allowed it to happen.
body.explanation: Without the last step the improvement decays. Commission on billing, credit terms set by sales, and cash reviewed monthly after the fact will rebuild the same position within about eighteen months, usually with better explanations attached.

body.title: The promoter has a faster idea
body.scenario: Six weeks in, collections are improving but slower than planned. The promoter proposes holding back ₹2.4 crore owed to micro and small suppliers for another 60 days, and using the GST collected this month to fund the wage bill, arguing that both are temporary, that the collections will catch up, and that "the suppliers know us, they will wait". He points out, correctly, that this would solve the immediate problem faster than anything in your plan.
body.prompt: He is right that it works. Why do you refuse, and what do you offer instead?
body.modelAnswer:
Agree with the premise and reject the conclusion, with numbers.
1. He is right that it releases cash fastest. That is exactly why it is dangerous: it is the cheapest-looking and most expensive option on the table.
2. Price the MSME delay. Interest under Section 16 of the MSMED Act runs at three times the RBI bank rate, compounded monthly, it is not deductible under Section 23, and the purchases stop being deductible until paid under Section 37(2)(g) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, formerly Section 43B(h) of the 1961 Act. The dues also get disclosed in MSME Form 1 and in the notes to the accounts, where the bank and the auditors will read them 60 days before the renewal.
3. Price the GST decision separately, because it is worse. That money was collected on behalf of the government and was never ours. It carries interest and late fees, the filing record is visible to customers and to the bank, and it is the single clearest signal in Lesson 6.2 that every cheaper option is exhausted.
4. Name the operational risk. One supplier has already stopped deliveries. If two more stop, the company cannot ship to its automotive customers, and losing an OEM approval takes years to recover, if ever.
Then offer the alternatives, because refusing without options is useless.
5. Discount more accepted invoices. The two large customers' invoices are exactly the asset that bill discounting and TReDS exist for, and pricing follows their credit rating, not ours.
6. Go to the bank now rather than at renewal, with the forecast and the six weeks of collections improvement. A temporary enhancement requested with evidence is a normal conversation.
7. Clear more dead stock, at a worse price if necessary. Cash today from an impaired asset beats interest on trust money.
8. Ask the promoter directly whether he will bring in funds, even short term. If the position is genuinely temporary, that is the cheapest bridge available and it signals commitment to both the bank and the team.
9. Accept a slower recovery. Ninety days becoming one hundred and twenty is survivable. A tax default, a stopped supply chain and an impaired banking relationship may not be.
10. Put the recommendation in writing, dated, with the numbers. If the decision goes the other way, that record matters.

body.title: The turnaround checklist
steps: Build a 13-week cash forecast from the actual bank balance, and identify the trough and its date.
Fund statutory dues first, permanently, and never treat collected tax as working capital.
Age receivables and assign every account beyond 60 days to a named owner with a date.
Age inventory and convert dead stock into cash at whatever it realistically fetches.
Separate micro and small suppliers in the payables ledger and pay them within the statutory limit.
Give large suppliers a written, dated schedule instead of silence.
Discount accepted invoices from strong buyers, or route them through TReDS, before seeking new borrowing.
Meet the bank early with data, ahead of any renewal or classification date.
Set twelve-month targets for debtor days, inventory days and payable days, and convert each into rupees.
Change the incentives, the credit approval route and the meeting rhythm, or the position will rebuild itself within eighteen months.

cards.definition: The first ninety days. Stop the bleeding, fund statutory dues, convert existing assets to cash.
A daily, named-owner push on overdue accounts, run by the people with the customer relationships.
Returning supplier payment to agreed and statutory terms. It consumes cash and is not optional.
Twelve-month targets on the three working capital levers, converted into rupees and owned by function.
Incentives, approval routes and meeting rhythm. Without it, improvements decay within about eighteen months.
Approaching lenders and suppliers with data before a deadline, when options are still cheap and still yours.

points: Vidarbha Engineering was profitable throughout. About ₹5.41 crore of six quarters' earnings went into receivables and stock rather than the bank.
Stabilise before you diagnose in detail: forecast, freeze discretionary spend, fund statutory dues, and convert existing assets into cash.
Ninety days produced ₹6.9 crore without a new lender, from collections, invoice discounting, deferred capex and dead stock.
The twelve-month plan releases about ₹5.40 crore and saves about ₹59 lakh of interest, roughly 11% of annual profit, with no additional sales.
Normalising supplier payment consumes ₹4.91 crore of that release. A plan that hides continued stretching is not a turnaround.
Change the incentives, the credit approval route and the weekly rhythm, or the same position rebuilds within about eighteen months.

body.text: Vidarbha Engineering is fictional and all figures are illustrative, calculated on constant annual sales for clarity. Statutory provisions are summarised for teaching and can change. Insolvency, tax and lending decisions require qualified professional advice specific to your situation. This is not legal, tax or investment advice.
